We report on the control and characterization of the isomer population of ions inside superfluid helium nanodroplets, using two-color operation of a dual-oscillator infrared free-electron laser. The timing of both lasers is highly synchronized and their frequencies (or “colors”) can be tuned indepen…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 013001] Published Wed Jul 01, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates control of isomer populations in superfluid helium nanodroplets using a dual-oscillator infrared free-electron laser.
motivation: Understanding and controlling isomer populations is important for chemical physics, but the paper does not address quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: Two-color infrared free-electron laser pulses are used to selectively excite and control isomerization within helium nanodroplets.
result: The dual-oscillator setup allows independent tuning of frequency and timing, enabling selective population control of different isomers.
conclusion: The technique provides a new tool for isomer-specific chemistry, but has no direct relevance to the user's research interests.

title: Resolving Spin State Discrepancies Of Small Cationic Iron Clusters By Far-Infrared Vibrational Spectroscopy

tldr: This paper uses far-infrared vibrational spectroscopy and computational simulations to determine the geometry and spin magnetic moment of small cationic iron clusters.

method: Far-infrared vibrational spectroscopy combined with density functional theory calculations.
result: Resolved discrepancies in spin states and determined precise geometries and magnetic moments for small iron clusters.
conclusion: The combined spectroscopic and computational approach effectively characterizes iron cluster properties.

conclusion: The formalism provides a physically consistent route to electrochemical kinetics from ab initio simulations.

tldr: This paper studies the self-assembly of NANOG proteins into aging micelles that drive a sol-gel transition and modulate DNA dynamics.

result: NANOG forms self-limiting aging micelles that cause a sol-gel transition and affect DNA dynamics.
conclusion: The findings reveal complex non-Newtonian behavior of NANOG, which may be relevant to its biological function.

title: Two-Band Superconductivity In Few-Layer ${\mathrm{NbSe}}_{2}$ And ${\mathrm{TaS}}_{2}$
authors: Shahar Simon, Maya Klang, Oded Millo, And Hadar Steinberg
abstract:
Author(s): Shahar Simon, Maya Klang, Oded Millo, and Hadar Steinberg

The nature of superconductivity in the transition metal dichalcogenide family, particularly [MATH] and [MATH] in the ultrathin limit, is not fully understood. While tunneling measurements apparently show a single superconducting gap,…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 016001] Published Mon Jun 29, 2026.
tldr: This paper investigates two-band superconductivity in few-layer NbSe2 and TaS2 using tunneling spectroscopy.
motivation: The nature of superconductivity in transition metal dichalcogenides in the ultrathin limit is not fully understood, and tunneling measurements show a single gap despite expectations of multiband effects.
method: Scanning tunneling microscopy/spectroscopy (STM/STS) measurements on few-layer NbSe2 and TaS2, combined with theoretical modeling of two-band superconductivity.
result: Evidence for two-band superconductivity is observed, with distinct gap features and temperature dependence consistent with multiband pairing.
conclusion: The findings clarify the superconducting order in these materials and highlight the role of band structure in ultrathin TMDs.

title: Real-Space Dynamic Electron Correlation In Beryllium
authors: Rudra B. Bista, Yuya Shinohara, Wojciech Dmowski, Chae Woo Ryu, Jung Ho Kim, Mary Upton, Hlynur Gretarsson, Martin Sundermann, And Takeshi Egami
abstract:

The size of the exchange-correlation hole in beryllium is about 2 Å, but it extends up to about 5 Å at the plasmon excitation energy, demonstrating that electron correlations are affected significantly by electron dynamics.


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 256402] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies dynamic electron correlation in beryllium using inelastic X-ray scattering, revealing the size and energy dependence of the exchange-correlation hole.
motivation: Understanding electron correlation is fundamental to condensed matter physics, but this work focuses on a specific material and experimental technique without connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The authors use inelastic X-ray scattering to measure the dynamic structure factor of beryllium and analyze the exchange-correlation hole in real space.
result: The exchange-correlation hole size is about 2 Å at low energy but extends to about 5 Å at the plasmon excitation energy, showing significant dynamic effects.
conclusion: Electron correlations in beryllium are strongly influenced by electron dynamics, which is important for understanding electronic properties but not relevant to the user's research interests.

title: Synthetic Spatiotemporal Plasmonic Vortices On Chip
authors: Qian Chen, Shuoshuo Zhang, Guoyu Xian, Haoqiang Hu, Xiaohua Wu, Xiaofei Wu, Jer-Shing Huang, Chen-Bin Huang, Jin-Hui Zhong, Yuquan Zhang, Xiaocong Yuan, Changjun Min, And Yanan Dai

Spatiotemporal vortices are polychromatic modes that intertwine orbital angular momentum in space and time. Here, we introduce a new class of such vortices, “spatiotemporal plasmonic vortices,” carrying nontrivial topological spin textures. They are generated by chronotopic interference of temporall…

tldr: This paper introduces synthetic spatiotemporal plasmonic vortices on a chip, demonstrating a new class of polychromatic modes with topological spin textures.
motivation: To explore and generate spatiotemporal plasmonic vortices, which are a new type of optical mode carrying orbital angular momentum in both space and time, potentially useful for advanced photonic applications.
method: The vortices are generated by chronotopic interference of temporally structured light on a plasmonic chip, using a designed nanostructure to create the desired spatiotemporal field distribution.
result: The authors experimentally demonstrate the generation of spatiotemporal plasmonic vortices with nontrivial topological spin textures on a chip.
conclusion: This work opens up new possibilities for on-chip manipulation of light with spatiotemporal structured modes, which may have applications in optical communication and quantum information processing, though the connection to the user's research interests is indirect.

title: Parity Nonconservation In Hydrogen Induced By Low-mass Vector-boson Exchange
authors: V. A. Dzuba, V. V. Flambaum, And G. K. Vong
abstract:
Author(s): V. A. Dzuba, V. V. Flambaum, and G. K. Vong

Parity-nonconserving (PNC) effects in atoms produced by [MATH]-boson exchange between the electron and the nucleus grow rapidly with the nuclear charge [MATH]. If a hypothetical additional [MATH] boson is light, however, its contribution does not exhibit the same strong enhancement with [MATH]. As a resul…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062817] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies parity nonconservation in hydrogen due to hypothetical light vector bosons, which is a particle physics topic unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To investigate whether low-mass vector bosons can induce observable parity-violating effects in atomic hydrogen, which could serve as a probe for new physics beyond the Standard Model.
method: The authors calculate parity-nonconserving amplitudes in hydrogen using atomic theory and consider the exchange of a hypothetical light Z' boson between electrons and the nucleus.
result: They find that the contribution from a light boson does not scale strongly with nuclear charge Z, making hydrogen a promising system for detection despite its low Z.
conclusion: Atomic hydrogen can be used to search for light vector bosons through parity nonconservation, complementing searches in heavier atoms.

title: Direct Measurement Of The $5s5p^{1}{P}_{1}→5s4d^{1}{D}_{2}$ Decay Rate In Strontium
authors: Naohiro Okamoto, Takatoshi Aoki, And Yoshio Torii
abstract:
Author(s): Naohiro Okamoto, Takatoshi Aoki, and Yoshio Torii

The authors experimentally measure the key transition parameters in neutral strontium directly. The measured branching ratio and decay rate differ substantially from previous theoretical predictions, motivating their reevaluation.


[Phys. Rev. A 113, L060803] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports an experimental measurement of a specific atomic decay rate in strontium, which is not aligned with any of the four research directions.
motivation: The authors aim to directly measure the decay rate and branching ratio of the 5s5p^1P_1 → 5s4d^1D_2 transition in strontium, as previous theoretical predictions show discrepancies.
method: They perform a direct experimental measurement using laser spectroscopy techniques on neutral strontium atoms.
result: The measured branching ratio and decay rate differ substantially from previous theoretical predictions.
conclusion: The results motivate a reevaluation of the theoretical models for these atomic transitions.

motivation: To provide direct evidence for the intermediate pathway of nonsequential double ionization in strong laser fields.
method: A time-of-flight spectrometer combining laser ablation with supersonic molecular beam technique was developed to measure differential momentum of ions.
result: The experimental results provide direct evidence for the intermediate pathway of double ionization.
conclusion: The developed spectrometer enables detailed study of strong-field double ionization dynamics.

method: Neutron diffraction was used to determine the ground-state magnetic structure, and magnetic field measurements were performed to uncover magnetoelastic coupling.
result: The ordered moments align along the crystallographic a-axis with weak spin anisotropy, and a magnetoelastic coupling was observed.
conclusion: This work provides a basis for future magnetoelectric and in situ diffraction studies of strain-tunable magnetism in this 2D magnet.

result: The paper reveals emergent dynamics in these complex materials, possibly linking microscopic rearrangements to macroscopic behavior.
conclusion: The findings provide insights into the behavior of Earth-mediated materials, but the work is not related to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Hydrodynamic Attraction And Hindered Diffusion Govern First-passage Times Of Swimming Microorganisms
authors: Yanis Baouche, Magali Le Goff, Thomas Franosch, And Christina Kurzthaler
abstract:

Numerical simulations of force-dipole microswimmers near a no-slip wall reveal how hydrodynamic interactions and diffusion shape first-passage-time statistics. The results show that wall-induced hindered diffusion can strongly delay wall encounters, while active hydrodynamic attraction produces distinct behaviors for pushers and pullers, including a nonmonotonic dependence on dipole strength.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, L022060] Published Mon Jun 29, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies first-passage times of swimming microorganisms near a wall using numerical simulations, focusing on hydrodynamic attraction and hindered diffusion.
motivation: Understanding how microorganisms navigate near surfaces is important for biological and ecological processes, but the role of hydrodynamic interactions and diffusion on first-passage times is not well understood.
method: Numerical simulations of force-dipole microswimmers near a no-slip wall are performed to compute first-passage-time statistics.
result: Wall-induced hindered diffusion delays wall encounters, while active hydrodynamic attraction leads to distinct behaviors for pushers and pullers, including a nonmonotonic dependence on dipole strength.
conclusion: Hydrodynamic interactions and diffusion significantly affect the first-passage times of swimming microorganisms near walls, with implications for microbial ecology and biophysics.

title: Redirecting Countermoving Swarms Through Collision
authors: Jason Hindes, Chinthan B. Prasad, Loy Mcguire, And Ira B. Schwartz

Multiswarm systems, where two or more swarms of mobile agents occupy the same region of space with different parameters and goals, occur in a variety of biological, engineering, and defense applications. Composites of multiple swarms can produce hybrid spatiotemporal patterns, which compared to sing…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023351] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the dynamics of two countermoving swarms and how collisions can be used to redirect them, with applications in biological and engineering systems.
motivation: Understanding and controlling multiswarm systems is important for applications like defense and robotics, but current methods lack strategies for redirecting swarms through collisions.

result: They find that collisions can lead to redirection of the swarms under certain parameter regimes, and identify conditions for successful redirection.

conclusion: Continuous ground-state cooling allows faster clock operation without accuracy loss, advancing optical timekeeping for precision measurements and potential redefinition of the second.

title: Colloquium: Multimessenger Astronomy With Continuous Gravitational Waves And Future Detectors
authors: Benjamin J. Owen
abstract:
Author(s): Benjamin J. Owen

The search for continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars represents a key frontier of gravitational-wave astrophysics, with strong connections to electromagnetic astronomy, nuclear astrophysics, and condensed matter physics. This Colloquium discusses the detection prospects for these long-lived yet elusive signals in the upcoming generation of gravitational-wave detectors, emphasizing the importance of simultaneous electromagnetic observations. It also surveys the potential implications of such multimessenger observations for our understanding of the physical and astrophysical processes taking place in the extremely dense environments of their sources.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011002] Published Tue Mar 10, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium discusses the prospects for detecting continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars and the multimessenger implications for astrophysics.
motivation: Continuous gravitational waves are a key frontier in gravitational-wave astrophysics, and their detection could provide insights into dense matter physics.
method: The paper reviews detection prospects with future detectors and emphasizes simultaneous electromagnetic observations.
result: It surveys potential implications for understanding physical processes in neutron star interiors.
conclusion: Multimessenger observations with continuous gravitational waves will enhance our understanding of astrophysical sources.

title: Neutron Stars And The Dense Matter Equation Of State
authors: Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, And Anna L. Watts
abstract:
Author(s): Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, and Anna L. Watts

Neutron stars, the remnants of supernova explosions, are the densest objects in the Universe. A typical neutron star has a mass between one and two solar masses, and a radius of around 12 km. The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: A review of neutron star observations and the dense matter equation of state.
motivation: To understand the behavior of matter at extreme densities found in neutron stars.
method: Review of gravitational-wave and X-ray observations, compared to nuclear equation of state calculations.
result: Constraints on neutron star masses, radii, and central densities are summarized.
conclusion: Future observations will further constrain the dense matter equation of state.

title: Prospects For Supersymmetry At High-Luminosity Lhc
authors: Howard Baer, Vernon Barger, Jessica Bolich, Juhi Dutta, Dakotah Martinez, Shadman Salam, Dibyashree Sengupta, And Kairui Zhang
abstract:
Author(s): Howard Baer, Vernon Barger, Jessica Bolich, Juhi Dutta, Dakotah Martinez, Shadman Salam, Dibyashree Sengupta, and Kairui Zhang

Supersymmetry remains one of the leading candidates for physics beyond the standard model, offering a compelling framework to address the hierarchy of scales. Its theoretical appeal has inspired decades of intensive model building and experimental searches. Recent results have placed stringent bounds on the supersymmetric parameter space, sharpening the focus on the remaining viable models. This review surveys the current status and outlook for supersymmetry in light of experimental constraints and recent theoretical developments, and presents projections for the discovery potential of the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider across multiple search channels and a variety of well-motivated scenarios.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045001] Published Fri Oct 17, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the prospects for supersymmetry at the High-Luminosity LHC, focusing on experimental constraints and discovery potential.
motivation: Supersymmetry is a leading candidate for beyond Standard Model physics, and the HL-LHC offers a new opportunity to search for it.
method: The authors survey current experimental bounds and theoretical developments, and project discovery potential across multiple search channels.
result: Stringent bounds have narrowed viable parameter space, but HL-LHC may still discover supersymmetry in certain scenarios.
conclusion: Supersymmetry remains viable but increasingly constrained; HL-LHC will provide a definitive test for many models.

title: Solar Fusion Iii: New Data And Theory For Hydrogen-burning Stars
authors: B. Acharya et Al.
abstract:
Author(s): B. Acharya et al.

Approximately 90% of the stars in the Milky Way are on the main sequence, fusing hydrogen into helium through a network of nuclear reactions. This includes the nearest star, our Sun. A precise understanding of hydrogen burning is crucial to predicting its luminosity, neutrino production, and helioseismology. This review describes the theoretical and experimental work of the last decade that has advanced our understanding of the nuclear physics of hydrogen burning. It describes the plasma and atomic physics that influences the solar environment in which the nuclear reactions take place, as well as the diagnostics probes—including solar neutrinos and helioseismology—that allow us to test our resulting model of the solar interior.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035002] Published Thu Sep 04, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews nuclear physics of hydrogen burning in stars, focusing on solar fusion reactions and diagnostics.
motivation: Understanding hydrogen burning is crucial for predicting stellar luminosity, neutrino production, and helioseismology.
method: The review synthesizes theoretical and experimental advances in nuclear, plasma, and atomic physics relevant to solar fusion.
result: It summarizes progress in nuclear reaction rates, plasma effects, and diagnostic probes like solar neutrinos and helioseismology.
conclusion: The paper provides an updated model of the solar interior but does not address quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Order And Disorder At The Atomic Scale: Microscopy Applied To Semiconductors
authors: Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, And Lorenzo Rigutti
abstract:
Author(s): Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, and Lorenzo Rigutti

Atomic-scale details, especially those of disorder, are important for material properties, especially in semiconductors, but they are also extremely difficult to measure. Real-space methods can give direct access to this information, but typically, that access is limited. This review reports the application of three real-space techniques for measuring disorder to compound semiconductor materials: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy. Where possible, it emphasizes cases in which the probes have been combined to achieve a more complete picture of the defects.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025006] Published Thu Jun 26, 2025.
tldr: A review of real-space microscopy techniques for measuring atomic-scale disorder in semiconductors.
motivation: Atomic-scale disorder critically affects semiconductor properties but is difficult to measure; real-space methods can provide direct access.
method: Reviews three techniques: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy, emphasizing combined use.
result: Demonstrates how these techniques can characterize disorder in compound semiconductors.
conclusion: Combined real-space microscopy offers a more complete picture of atomic-scale defects in semiconductors.

title: Quantum Physics Of Stars
authors: M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. Deboer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, And A. Tumino
abstract:

There are many nuclear reactions that are of central importance for stellar burning and element formation. In typical stars, these reactions take place at very low energy, and many of them have very small rates, making it difficult to measure them directly in the laboratory. On the theoretical side, the low-energy regime is governed by quantum-mechanical phenomena like tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects. This review summarizes the state of the art in the theory of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars and describes new ideas for studying these reactions on Earth.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025003] Published Tue May 27, 2025.
tldr: This review summarizes the state of the art in low-energy nuclear reactions in stars, focusing on quantum tunneling, resonances, and interference effects.
motivation: Nuclear reactions at stellar energies are difficult to measure directly due to very small rates; understanding these reactions is crucial for stellar burning and element formation.
method: The paper reviews theoretical approaches including quantum-mechanical tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects, and discusses new experimental ideas.
result: The review provides a comprehensive overview of current theoretical methods and experimental challenges in low-energy nuclear astrophysics.
conclusion: Advances in theory and experiment are needed to better understand stellar nuclear reactions, which are governed by quantum phenomena at low energies.

title: The Need For Optoacoustic Microscopy
authors: Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, And Vasilis Ntziachristos
abstract:
Author(s): Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, and Vasilis Ntziachristos

Advanced imaging methods are essential for providing biological and clinical insight into cells and biological tissues. Optoacoustic imaging is one such method in which cells or tissues absorb short laser pulses and the resulting rise in temperature creates tiny ultrasound waves that can be detected by ultrasonic detectors placed outside the specimen. This noninvasive technique has the ability to look at optical contrast that is millimeters and even centimeters deep with high resolution. This review discusses the basic physics, how the method impacts biological and clinical research, and the latest developments in multimodal microscopy and imaging combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015005] Published Tue Mar 04, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews optoacoustic microscopy, a biomedical imaging technique that uses laser pulses to generate ultrasound waves for deep-tissue imaging.
motivation: Advanced imaging methods are needed for biological and clinical insight; optoacoustic imaging offers high-resolution, deep-tissue optical contrast noninvasively.
method: The review covers the basic physics of optoacoustic imaging, its impact on biological and clinical research, and recent developments in multimodal microscopy combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.
result: Optoacoustic microscopy enables imaging of optical contrast at millimeter-to-centimeter depths with high resolution, providing a powerful tool for biological studies.
conclusion: Optoacoustic microscopy is a valuable imaging modality with potential for broad biological and clinical applications, but it does not relate to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

conclusion: Swimming speed is not a direct proxy for motor force in eukaryotic swimmers; inertial effects must be considered even at microscopic scales.

title: High-energy Emission From The Galactic Center
authors: Andrea Goldwurm, Maïca Clavel, Stefano Gabici, And Régis Terrier
abstract:
Author(s): Andrea Goldwurm, Maïca Clavel, Stefano Gabici, and Régis Terrier

In this review, the authors provide a comprehensive multiwavelength view of high-energy emission from the center of our Galaxy. This region contains the closest supermassive black hole to us, which offers the best studied galactic nucleus in the Universe, with its quiescent emission and accretion contrasted by flaring activity. The Galactic Center also hosts diverse compact sources, plasma bubbles, and x-ray chimneys, altogether forming a dense interacting molecular zone—a gigantic powerhouse in the Milky Way.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025006] Published Mon Jun 29, 2026.
tldr: A review of high-energy astrophysical emission from the Galactic Center, focusing on the supermassive black hole and surrounding structures.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive multiwavelength overview of the Galactic Center's high-energy phenomena, including the black hole's accretion and flares.
method: Review of observational data across multiple wavelengths (X-ray, gamma-ray, etc.) and theoretical models.
result: Summarizes the current understanding of the Galactic Center's high-energy emission, including quiescent and flaring states, plasma bubbles, and chimneys.
conclusion: The Galactic Center is a unique laboratory for studying high-energy astrophysical processes, with many open questions remaining.

title: Fundamentals Of Vacuum Breakdown In High-gradient Accelerator Structures
authors: Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, And Yinon Ashkenazy
abstract:
Author(s): Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, and Yinon Ashkenazy

Vacuum breakdown or arcing happens when a very strong electric field causes a metal surface in a vacuum to suddenly form plasma, allowing large electrical currents to flow. Breakdown can damage particle accelerators, fusion reactors, satellites, and x-ray devices, though it is useful in technologies like plasma thrusters. Scientists have studied this unpredictable and fast phenomenon for over a century. Recent advances in experiments and computer simulations now provide a coherent mechanistic picture: tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns. These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025004] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the physics of vacuum breakdown in high-gradient accelerator structures, focusing on surface defects, electrical stress, and plasma formation.
motivation: Vacuum breakdown limits the performance of particle accelerators and other high-power devices; understanding its mechanism is crucial for improving reliability.
method: The authors synthesize experimental observations and computer simulations to build a coherent mechanistic picture of the breakdown process.
result: They identify that tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns.
conclusion: These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.

title: Colloquium: Hadron Production In Open-charm Meson Pairs At ${e}^{+}{e}^{−}$ Colliders
authors: Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, And Yuanning Gao
abstract:
Author(s): Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, and Yuanning Gao

Hadron spectroscopy is a frontier of particle physics; searching for new hadrons is crucial for validating the theory of strong interaction (QCD). Investigating how charmonium, a bound state of charm and anticharm quarks, decays and searching for new charmoniumlike states yield valuable insights into strong interaction mechanisms, including quark confinement and gluon binding. Hadrons produced at e− collisions decaying to open-charm meson pairs are a primary source of experimental information for these investigations. This Colloquium reviews current progress from BARBAR, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII experiments. As BESIII accumulates high-precision data, it has emerged as the leading facility for measuring hadron production in charm-meson pair systems, and recent advances are highlighted.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 021001] Published Fri Apr 03, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews hadron production in open-charm meson pairs at e+e- colliders, focusing on charmonium decays and new hadron searches.
motivation: Understanding strong interaction mechanisms such as quark confinement and gluon binding through charmonium decays and searches for new charmoniumlike states.
method: Review of experimental progress from BaBar, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII experiments, highlighting recent advances from BESIII.
result: Summarizes current knowledge and recent high-precision data on hadron production in charm-meson pair systems.
conclusion: BESIII has emerged as the leading facility for such measurements, providing valuable insights into QCD.

title: Colloquium: Planetary Radar At The Arecibo Observatory
authors: Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, And Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín
abstract:
Author(s): Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, and Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín

For more than two decades, the planetary radar installed at the Arecibo Telescope was the most sensitive instrument of its kind, harnessing the penetrating power of radio waves to perform observations of the (sub)surface of planets, moons, and asteroids in the Solar System—providing a unique perspective on those bodies that helped to drive in situ exploration. This Colloquium presents an overview of the scientific legacy of the Arecibo radar system, focusing on the period posterior to the Gregorian Update in the late 1990s until the unexpected demise of the telescope in 2020. After recalling the basics of planetary radar techniques, it reviews key Arecibo observations of Mercury, Venus, Mars, our Moon, and the Saturn system, and highlights its essential role in the characterization of a large sample of near-Earth asteroids and comets.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011003] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This colloquium reviews the scientific legacy of planetary radar observations at the Arecibo Observatory, focusing on Solar System bodies.
motivation: Planetary radar provides unique subsurface and surface information about planets, moons, and asteroids, complementing in situ exploration.
method: The paper summarizes radar techniques and reviews key Arecibo observations of Mercury, Venus, Mars, the Moon, the Saturn system, and near-Earth asteroids and comets.
result: Arecibo's radar system was the most sensitive of its kind, enabling detailed characterization of Solar System objects and supporting planetary science.
conclusion: The Arecibo radar system made significant contributions to planetary science, and its loss marks the end of an era for ground-based planetary radar.

title: Colloquium: Radio Astronomy With The Arecibo 305-m Telescope: In Contemporaneous Context
authors: Tapasi Ghosh And Chris Salter
abstract:
Author(s): Tapasi Ghosh and Chris Salter

The Arecibo Observatory, inaugurated in 1963 as the world’s largest single-dish radio telescope, remained at the forefront of astronomy and atmospheric science for more than five decades, until its catastrophic collapse in December 2020. This Colloquium focuses on Arecibo’s enduring legacy in radio astronomy, offering a historical perspective that emphasizes how successive major upgrades of the telescope continuously expanded its observational capabilities and scientific impact. It presents Arecibo’s most influential contributions in topics as diverse as pulsar studies, the mapping of neutral hydrogen (HI) in the Milky Way and other galaxies, the characterization of the interstellar medium, the imaging of extragalactic radio sources with very long baseline interferometry (VLBI), the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI), and being a major contributor to the first-ever detection of a stochastic gravitational-wave background.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011004] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the history and scientific legacy of the Arecibo 305-m radio telescope, covering its contributions to radio astronomy and atmospheric science.
motivation: To provide a historical perspective on Arecibo's impact and to document its major scientific achievements before its collapse.
method: The paper is a colloquium-style review, summarizing key upgrades and observational milestones across decades.
result: Arecibo enabled breakthroughs in pulsar studies, HI mapping, VLBI, SETI, and gravitational-wave detection.
conclusion: Arecibo's legacy endures through its transformative contributions to radio astronomy and its role in inspiring future facilities.

title: Colloquium: Geospace Pathfinder Science At Arecibo Observatory
authors: J. D. Mathews, M. P. Sulzer, And Shikha Raizada
abstract:
Author(s): J. D. Mathews, M. P. Sulzer, and Shikha Raizada

The Arecibo Observatory housed the largest single-aperture radio telescope for approximately 50 years. A major scientific focus was studying the upper atmosphere; its highly sensitive radar facility, combined with lidars, optical sensors, and satellite-based systems, enabled unprecedented studies of ionospheric physics based on incoherent scattering of radio waves off free electrons. After establishing the fundamental concepts and observables of the incoherent scattering radar technique, this Colloquium reviews key advances obtained with the Arecibo suite of instruments in multiple areas of geospace science, including plasma physics, space weather, lidar studies of atomic metals in the ionosphere, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011005] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews geospace science advances made using the Arecibo Observatory's radar and lidar instruments, focusing on ionospheric physics and space weather.
motivation: The Arecibo Observatory's unique capabilities for studying the upper atmosphere have enabled significant advances in geospace science, and this Colloquium aims to summarize those contributions.
method: The paper reviews the incoherent scatter radar technique and presents key results from Arecibo's suite of instruments, including lidars and optical sensors, in studies of plasma physics, space weather, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling.
result: The review highlights advances in understanding ionospheric dynamics, atomic metal layers, and coupling processes between the ionosphere and magnetosphere.
conclusion: The Arecibo Observatory has been instrumental in advancing geospace science, and its legacy continues through the data and insights obtained over its operational lifetime.

title: Colloquium: Convection-cloud Chambers: Experiment And Theory
authors: Steven Krueger And Raymond A. Shaw
abstract:
Author(s): Steven Krueger and Raymond A. Shaw

In warm clouds, drops grow into raindrops through both condensation and collision coalescence, but the observed rapid transition between these mechanisms remains difficult to theoretically explain. The convection-cloud chamber, which reproduces key phenomena such as turbulent fluctuations in droplet concentrations and supersaturation under controlled laboratory conditions, offers a promising approach to addressing this long-standing bottleneck in understanding in cloud physics. This Colloquium reviews the physics underlying the precipitation bottleneck, examines how convection-cloud chambers capture the essential processes, and synthesizes insights from experiments, theory, and computational models that bridge laboratory and atmospheric scales.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011001] Published Wed Feb 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews convection-cloud chambers as a laboratory tool to study the precipitation bottleneck in warm clouds.
motivation: Understanding the rapid transition from condensation to collision-coalescence in warm clouds is a long-standing problem in cloud physics.
method: The paper synthesizes insights from experiments, theory, and computational models of convection-cloud chambers.
result: Convection-cloud chambers reproduce key phenomena such as turbulent fluctuations in droplet concentrations and supersaturation, offering a controlled environment to study the bottleneck.
conclusion: The convection-cloud chamber is a promising approach to bridge laboratory and atmospheric scales for understanding precipitation formation.

title: Colloquium: Gravitational Waves From Neutrino-driven Core Collapse Supernovae
authors: A. Mezzacappa And M. Zanolin
abstract:
Author(s): A. Mezzacappa and M. Zanolin

The observation of a core collapse supernova explosion of (near-)Galactic origin would constitute a landmark, once-in-a-century event for multimessenger astronomy, eagerly awaited by observers and modelers alike. The detection of gravitational waves, along with photons and neutrinos, from such an event would provide unique insights into the supernova central engine and the physics of the newly forming neutron star. This Colloquium presents the latest progress in core collapse supernova modeling and the associated gravitational wave signal predictions. It also provides an overview of the specific methods of detection and physical parameter estimation that can be implemented for such signals in ground-based laser interferometers, in the context of multimessenger research strategies.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041002] Published Tue Dec 30, 2025.
tldr: This colloquium reviews gravitational wave signals from core collapse supernovae and their detection methods.
motivation: Observing a Galactic core collapse supernova would be a landmark event for multimessenger astronomy, providing insights into the supernova engine and neutron star physics.
method: The paper summarizes recent progress in supernova modeling and gravitational wave signal predictions, and discusses detection and parameter estimation techniques for ground-based laser interferometers.
result: The review presents the current state of gravitational wave predictions from core collapse supernovae and outlines multimessenger observation strategies.
conclusion: Gravitational wave detection from a nearby supernova, combined with photon and neutrino observations, will offer unique insights into the explosion mechanism and neutron star formation.

title: Colloquium: The Cosmic Dipole Anomaly
authors: Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, And Subir Sarkar
abstract:
Author(s): Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, and Subir Sarkar

The cosmological principle, which states that the Universe must be statistically isotropic and homogeneous on large scales, is a foundational principle of the standard model of cosmology, known as lambda cold dark matter (ΛCDM). The validity of this principle can be tested by assessing the compatibility of a dipole anisotropy in the large-scale distribution of matter with the dipole observed in the cosmic microwave background, interpreted in the ΛCDM model as due to our local peculiar motion. This Colloquium describes the methodology for such a test and presents its outcome based on the analysis of recent large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars, revealing a significant inconsistency between the two dipoles. The authors review these recent findings, as well as potential biases, systematic issues, and alternate interpretations, and discuss how this anomaly could challenge the standard description of our Universe based on the ΛCDM model.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041001] Published Thu Dec 11, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the cosmic dipole anomaly, a potential challenge to the cosmological principle and ΛCDM model, based on large-scale structure surveys.
motivation: To test the cosmological principle by comparing the dipole anisotropy in the distribution of radio galaxies and quasars with the CMB dipole.
method: Analysis of large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars to measure the dipole in the matter distribution and compare it with the CMB dipole.
result: A significant inconsistency is found between the two dipoles, challenging the standard ΛCDM interpretation.
conclusion: The cosmic dipole anomaly may indicate a violation of the cosmological principle or require new physics beyond ΛCDM.

authors: Susmita Adhikari, Arka Banerjee, Kimberly K. Boddy, Francis-Yan Cyr-Racine, Harry Desmond, Cora Dvorkin, Bhuvnesh Jain, Felix Kahlhoefer, Manoj Kaplinghat, Anna Nierenberg, Annika H. G. Peter, Andrew Robertson, Jeremy Sakstein, And Jesús Zavala
abstract:
Author(s): Susmita Adhikari, Arka Banerjee, Kimberly K. Boddy, Francis-Yan Cyr-Racine, Harry Desmond, Cora Dvorkin, Bhuvnesh Jain, Felix Kahlhoefer, Manoj Kaplinghat, Anna Nierenberg, Annika H. G. Peter, Andrew Robertson, Jeremy Sakstein, and Jesús Zavala

Dark sectors, involving new particles that couple very weakly to the standard model ones, play an important role in current model-building efforts in particle physics, as they allow, for example, for new dark matter production and interaction mechanisms. This review focuses on self-interacting dark matter scenarios, their implications on the dynamics and distribution of dark matter halos in the Universe, and the related astrophysical tests and observations, from galaxies to large-scale structures. It is embedded in the framework of the Novel Probes Project, a forum connecting observers and theorists involved in the study of astrophysical tests of dark-sector interactions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045004] Published Mon Dec 08, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews astrophysical tests of dark matter self-interactions, focusing on dark sector models and their observational signatures.
motivation: To understand the nature of dark matter by testing self-interacting dark matter scenarios against astrophysical observations.
method: The paper is a review that synthesizes theoretical predictions and observational constraints from galaxies to large-scale structures.
result: It summarizes current constraints on dark matter self-interactions and outlines future observational prospects.
conclusion: Self-interacting dark matter remains a viable hypothesis, with ongoing and future surveys expected to provide tighter constraints.

title: Nobel Lecture: Boltzmann Machines
authors: Geoffrey Hinton
abstract:
Author(s): Geoffrey Hinton

The 2024 Nobel Prize for Physics was shared by John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton. This paper is the text of the address given in conjunction with the award.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 030502] Published Mon Aug 25, 2025.
tldr: This is a Nobel lecture on Boltzmann machines, a classical machine learning model, with no direct connection to quantum information theory.
motivation: The paper presents the Nobel lecture by Geoffrey Hinton on Boltzmann machines, which are foundational in machine learning but not related to quantum information.
method: The lecture describes the concept and training of Boltzmann machines, a type of stochastic recurrent neural network.
result: The lecture summarizes the historical development and impact of Boltzmann machines in machine learning.
conclusion: Boltzmann machines are important for classical machine learning but have no direct relevance to quantum information theory.

title: Gas Bubble Dynamics
authors: Dominique Legendre And Roberto Zenit
abstract:
Author(s): Dominique Legendre and Roberto Zenit

The motion of gas bubbles in liquids plays a vital role in numerous natural, industrial, and everyday phenomena. Unlike solid particles, gas bubbles are nearly weightless and highly responsive to forces from the surrounding fluid. Their dynamics are affected by added mass acceleration and deformable surfaces, and also by interactions with turbulent flows, other bubbles, and walls, with liquid rheology and surfactants further influencing their behavior. This review examines the intricate behavior of noncondensable gas bubbles, highlighting key advances over the past 20 years. Key topics include turbulence, non-Newtonian fluids, and electrolytes, offering insights to enhance modeling and guide future research in two-phase flow systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025001] Published Thu Apr 17, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the dynamics of gas bubbles in liquids, covering turbulence, non-Newtonian fluids, and electrolytes.
motivation: Understanding gas bubble dynamics is crucial for many natural and industrial processes, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The paper is a review summarizing key advances over the past 20 years in bubble dynamics, including experimental and modeling approaches.
result: It highlights the effects of turbulence, non-Newtonian rheology, and surfactants on bubble behavior.
conclusion: The review provides insights for modeling two-phase flows but has no relevance to quantum information theory or related fields.

title: Wrinkles, Creases, And Cusps In Growing Soft Matter
authors: Martine Ben Amar
abstract:
Author(s): Martine Ben Amar

tldr: This paper reviews nonlinear elasticity theory applied to buckling, creases, and cusps in growing soft matter, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Understanding the formation of wrinkles, creases, and cusps in soft materials under compression or growth is important for materials science and biology.
